lessons.title: Falling intonation
lessons.explain: Your pitch drops at the end. It sounds finished, certain and confident.

lessons.title: Rising intonation
lessons.explain: Your pitch goes up at the end. It sounds like a question, a check or an unfinished thought.

items.text: I bought bread, milk, and eggs.

lessons.title: Rise-fall and fall-rise
lessons.explain: These two patterns carry attitude: surprise, doubt, politeness or a hidden 'but'.

lessons.title: Question tags: checking vs asking
lessons.explain: The same tag question can mean two different things depending on whether your pitch rises or falls at the end.
points: Falling tag = I'm almost sure, just confirming.
Rising tag = I'm genuinely not sure, really asking.

items.text: You locked the door, didn't you? ↗

lessons.title: Or-questions: two different meanings
lessons.explain: 'Or' questions change meaning completely depending on the final pitch movement.
points: Rising on the last option = yes/no question about both together.
Falling on the last option = choose one of the two.

items.text: Do you want tea or coffee? ↘
Do you want tea or coffee? ↗
items.note: Asks: do you want a drink at all (either one)?

lessons.title: Exclamations
lessons.explain: Exclamations use a big pitch jump to show strong feeling — surprise, excitement or admiration.

lessons.title: Lists with more than two items
lessons.explain: Every item in a list rises except the last one, which falls to show the list is finished.

items.text: I need apples, bananas, oranges, and milk.
We visited Paris, Rome, and Berlin.

lessons.title: Echo questions for surprise
lessons.explain: Repeating part of what someone said, with a sharp rise, shows surprise or disbelief.

items.text: A: I moved to Iceland. B: You moved WHERE? ↗
A: I quit my job. B: You did WHAT? ↗
A: It cost two thousand dollars. B: TWO THOUsand? ↗

lessons.title: Polite requests with fall-rise softening
lessons.explain: A gentle fall-rise on a request sounds more polite and less like a demand.

lessons.title: Intonation in giving choices
lessons.explain: Offering two or more options in a sentence uses rise-then-fall, just like a two-item list.

items.text: You can pay by card or cash.
We can meet today or tomorrow.

lessons.title: Intonation for genuine uncertainty
lessons.explain: A rising or level pitch on a statement (instead of falling) signals you're not fully sure.

items.text: I think it's around five o'clock? ↗

lessons.title: Intonation in greetings
lessons.explain: A warm, falling intonation on greetings sounds friendly and confident.

items.note: Rising here sounds casual and friendly, not like a real question.

lessons.title: Intonation for sarcasm and irony
lessons.explain: Sarcastic tone usually exaggerates the pitch and stretches the stressed word longer than normal.

items.note: The word 'great' is stretched and falls hard — the opposite of sincere.

items.text: Yeah, that's exactly what I wanted.

lessons.title: Intonation in giving good news vs bad news
lessons.explain: A wide pitch range signals good news; a narrower, lower range signals bad news.

items.text: Guess what — I got the job!
I'm sorry, but we didn't get approved.

lessons.title: Intonation across a whole IELTS-style answer
lessons.explain: A long spoken answer should still fall clearly at the very end of each main idea, even with several sentences.

items.text: I think travelling is important because it broadens your perspective, and it also helps you understand other cultures better.

lessons.title: Declarative questions (statement form, question meaning)
lessons.explain: A statement with rising intonation can become a genuine question without changing the word order at all.

items.text: This is your first time here? ↗

lessons.title: Intonation reading out numbers and phone numbers
lessons.explain: Each group of digits rises slightly except the very last group, which falls to show you've finished.

items.text: five five five ↗ one two three four ↘
My number is oh two one ↗ five five five ↘

lessons.title: Intonation in warnings
lessons.explain: Warnings often use a sharp rise-fall on the danger word to grab attention immediately.

lessons.title: Intonation for reassurance
lessons.explain: A calm, gently falling pitch with a soft final tone sounds comforting and reassuring.

items.text: Don't worry, everything will be fine.
items.pattern: don't WORry, everything will be FINE ↘

lessons.title: Intonation when giving a compliment
lessons.explain: Genuine compliments use a warm rise-fall to sound sincere rather than flat or sarcastic.

lessons.title: Intonation closing small talk politely
lessons.explain: Ending a conversation politely uses a gentle, falling, friendly tone.

items.text: Well, it was great catching up.
items.pattern: well, it was GREAT catching UP ↘

lessons.title: Intonation while negotiating
lessons.explain: Negotiating uses fall-rise a lot — firm but leaving room for discussion.

items.text: I could do fifty, but not sixty. ↘↗
That's a bit more than I wanted to spend. ↘↗

lessons.title: Intonation when explaining steps to someone
lessons.explain: Teaching intonation rises slightly at the end of each step to show 'more is coming' and falls on the last step.

items.text: First you open the app, ↗ then you log in, ↗ and finally you tap submit. ↘

lessons.title: Same words, different intonation, different meaning
lessons.explain: Identical words can be a plain statement or a real question — only the pitch tells you which.

lessons.title: Intonation in a sincere apology
lessons.explain: Sincere apologies fall gently and slowly — a flat or fast fall can sound insincere.

items.pattern: I'm REALly SORry about THAT ↘ (slow, gentle fall)

lessons.title: Enthusiasm vs boredom: same sentence, opposite energy
lessons.explain: The exact same words can sound excited or bored depending only on pitch range and speed.

lessons.title: Intonation in a formal announcement
lessons.explain: Formal announcements use clear, wide falls on each main point to sound authoritative and easy to follow.

items.text: Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for joining us today.
The meeting will begin in five minutes.

lessons.title: Continuing intonation mid-sentence
lessons.explain: A slight rise or level pitch in the middle of a sentence signals 'I'm not finished yet.'

items.text: When I got home ↗, I made dinner ↘.
items.pattern: level/rise mid-sentence, fall at the end

items.text: Even though it was late ↗, we kept working ↘.

lessons.title: Intonation when checking you understood correctly
lessons.explain: Checking understanding uses a rising tag or a rising echo to invite confirmation.

items.text: So you're saying we should wait? ↗
If I understood right, the deadline is Friday? ↗

lessons.title: Intonation when offering help
lessons.explain: Offers of help usually rise gently, sounding open and inviting rather than pushy.

items.text: Can I help you with that?
items.pattern: can I HELP you with THAT ↗

items.text: Would you like me to carry that?
items.pattern: would you LIKE me to CARry that ↗

lessons.title: Intonation expressing disappointment
lessons.explain: Disappointment often uses a falling pitch that starts lower than usual and drops further, sounding flat and deflated.

items.text: Oh. I was really hoping we could go.

lessons.title: Intonation in giving clear instructions
lessons.explain: Instructions fall clearly at the end of each command so the listener knows exactly when one instruction ends.

items.text: Turn left. ↘ Then go straight. ↘ Stop at the light. ↘

lessons.title: Intonation building to a storytelling climax
lessons.explain: The pitch rises and the pace quickens as a story builds tension, then falls sharply at the climax.

items.text: And then... ↗ the door slowly opened... ↗ and there was NOBODY there! ↗↘
items.pattern: rising tension, sharp fall-rise at the climax

lessons.title: Intonation showing confusion
lessons.explain: Confusion often uses a rising, questioning tone even on statements, with a slight pause before.

items.text: Hold on, what do you mean? ↗

lessons.title: Intonation in a polite disagreement
lessons.explain: Disagreeing politely often starts with a fall-rise to soften it before the falling main point.

items.text: I see what you mean, ↘↗ but I'm not sure I agree. ↘
items.pattern: fall-rise softener, then falling main point

items.text: That's a fair point, ↘↗ though I'd look at it differently. ↘

lessons.title: Intonation reading a list vs a casual list
lessons.explain: A formal, careful list uses clear rises on each item; a casual list runs the items together more.

items.text: We need eggs, ↗ milk, ↗ butter, ↗ and flour. ↘

items.pattern: casual, fast, one small fall at the end

lessons.title: Intonation correcting someone politely
lessons.explain: A gentle fall-rise softens a correction so it doesn't sound like an attack.

items.text: Actually, I think it's the other way around. ↘↗
Just to clarify, the meeting's at three, not four. ↘↗

lessons.title: Intonation giving a toast
lessons.explain: A toast uses a warm, rising build-up followed by a strong, confident fall on the final wish.

items.text: To all of you, ↗ to good times, ↗ and to many more years ahead! ↘

lessons.title: Intonation expressing relief
lessons.explain: Relief often starts high and falls with a long, relaxed glide, almost like a sigh.

lessons.title: Intonation introducing yourself formally vs casually
lessons.explain: A formal introduction falls in a measured, even way; a casual one is faster with a friendlier rise.

items.text: Good morning, my name is Sarah Johnson.

lessons.title: Intonation cheering someone on
lessons.explain: Encouragement uses an energetic rise-fall to sound genuinely supportive.

lessons.title: Intonation in a job interview answer
lessons.explain: Confident interview answers fall clearly and firmly at the end of each key point.

items.text: I believe my experience makes me a strong fit for this role.

lessons.title: Intonation with contrast markers (however, but)
lessons.explain: A slight rise or pause before 'however' or 'but' signals a contrast is coming.

items.text: The plan sounds good, ↗ however, there's one issue. ↘
It's cheap, ↗ but the quality isn't great. ↘

lessons.title: Intonation asking permission
lessons.explain: Asking permission almost always rises to sound open and non-demanding.

items.text: Is it okay if I leave early? ↗

lessons.title: Intonation delivering bad news gently
lessons.explain: Gentle bad news uses a soft, slow fall — a sudden hard fall can sound cold or blunt.

items.text: I'm afraid we won't be able to approve this.

lessons.title: Intonation showing indifference
lessons.explain: A flat, narrow pitch with little movement signals 'I don't really care either way.'

items.text: I guess it's fine, whatever works.
Either one is okay with me.

lessons.title: Intonation reading prices and quantities
lessons.explain: Prices fall clearly on the final amount to sound definite and easy to note down.

items.text: It comes to about forty euros. ↘

lessons.title: Intonation calling someone across a room
lessons.explain: Calling someone's name to get attention uses a wide rise-fall so it carries and stands out.

lessons.title: Intonation in a countdown
lessons.explain: A countdown rises with anticipation on each number and falls sharply on the final word.

lessons.title: Final mixed review: pick the right pattern
lessons.explain: A closing mixed set — decide falling, rising, rise-fall or fall-rise for each line before checking.

items.text: That's the end of the tour.
